mainTopic: רבי's ruling about meat in gentile butcher shops, and רב's rule that meat which went out of sight is forbidden
overview: The amud opens at the end of a story about a quarrel. A butcher claims that the meat his rival got through a gentile came from a טְרֵפָה ox. רבי refuses to forbid all the butcher shops because of one fool, which fits his rule: where the butchers are Jewish, meat found with a gentile is permitted. In a second version, the butcher only said this to hurt his rival. The גמרא explains that this version needs that reason because here a forbidden sale had been put on record. The גמרא then brings רב's rule that meat which went out of sight is forbidden, and tests it against several sources. It answers some by saying the meat was found in a gentile's hand or was watched the whole time. For the last source, רב reads 'permitted' as meaning only free from נבלה status. Finally, the גמרא reveals that רב's rule was only inferred, and begins the story of רב at the river, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The butcher taunts his rival, who says he ate the meat anyway
steps.stepSummary: The butcher tells the man he quarreled with that if he had made peace, he would have gotten meat from the fattened ox. The man answers that he ate the best of it anyway, through a gentile.
steps.simpleTranslation: The butcher said: 'If you had made up with me, wouldn't I have given you some of the fattened ox I prepared yesterday?' The other man answered: 'I ate the very best of it anyway.' The butcher asked: 'How did you get it?' He answered: 'A certain gentile bought it and fed it to me.'
steps.whatsHappening: The story, which began earlier, continues with a back-and-forth between the butcher and the man he quarreled with. This sets up the butcher's surprising claim in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The butcher is rubbing it in: 'You lost out because you wouldn't make peace.' The other man answers that he got the meat anyway, through a gentile who bought it from the butcher. That detail matters, because it means meat from a Jewish butcher ended up with a gentile and then was eaten by a Jew.

keyTerms.meaning: To make peace or make up with someone
A fattened ox, the best kind of meat
The finest of the fine, the very best part
From where did you get it?

phrases.english: If you had made peace with me,
phrases.notes: The butcher is speaking to the man he had a quarrel with. The story started before this point.

phrases.english: wouldn't I have fed you
from the fattened ox that I prepared yesterday?
He said to him: I ate from the finest of the fine.
phrases.notes: He means: I ate the best of that same ox anyway.

phrases.english: He said to him: From where did you get it?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: דִּזְבַן פְּלוֹנִי גּוֹי וּסְפָא לִי.
phrases.english: He said to him: So-and-so the gentile bought it and fed it to me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a story that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat from the butcher's ox reached a Jew by way of a gentile buyer.

steps.title: The butcher claims the meat sold to the gentile was טְרֵפָה
steps.stepSummary: The butcher answers that he prepared two oxen, and the one that went to the gentile was a טְרֵפָה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The butcher said: 'I prepared two oxen, and that one was a טְרֵפָה.'
steps.whatsHappening: The butcher hits back by saying the meat his rival ate was not kosher. This claim is what creates the halachic problem רבי will respond to next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If this is true, then a Jewish butcher sold non-kosher meat to a gentile, and Jews later ate it from the gentile. That would seem to show that meat in gentile hands cannot be trusted as kosher, even in a town with Jewish butchers.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect, which may not be eaten even after שחיטה

phrases.english: He said to him: I prepared two,
phrases.notes: He means two oxen. One was kosher and one was not.

phrases.english: and that one was a tereifa.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The butcher's reply to the man's boast in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The butcher claims the ox sold to the gentile was a טְרֵפָה.

steps.title: רבי refuses to forbid all butcher shops because of one fool
steps.stepSummary: רבי says that one fool acting improperly is no reason to forbid the meat in all the butcher shops.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי said: 'Because of this fool who acted improperly, should we forbid all the butcher shops?!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי gives his reaction to the story. He will not forbid the meat sold in the butcher shops just because of what this butcher did.
steps.deeperAnalysis: One could think that this story proves meat with gentiles might be טְרֵפָה, so it should all be forbidden. רבי says no: in this version, the butcher really did act improperly, but one fool's bad behavior does not change the general rule.
steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that a general חזקה is not overturned by one unusual act of misconduct.

phrases.english: Rabbi said:
Because of this fool
who acted improperly,
should we forbid all the butcher shops?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: רבי's halachic reaction to the butcher's claim.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat in the butcher shops stays permitted despite one butcher's improper act.

steps.title: רבי's ruling fits his known view on meat found with a gentile
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says רבי is consistent. He holds that where the butcher shops and butchers are Jewish, meat found with a gentile is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי follows his own reasoning, since he said: 'Where there are butcher shops and Jewish butchers, meat found in a gentile's hand is permitted.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא connects רבי's reaction to a ruling he gave elsewhere. This shows his response in the story is not a one-time decision.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי's general rule is that when the butchers in a place are Jewish, meat in a gentile's hands can be assumed to come from them and to be kosher. Since that is his rule, he would not throw it out because of one butcher's story.

keyTerms.meaning: Following his own reasoning, consistent with his known view
In the hand (possession) of a gentile

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי permits all meat held by gentiles anywhere. His rule is about a place where the butcher shops and butchers are Jewish.

phrases.english: Rabbi follows his own reasoning, as he said:
Where there are butcher shops and Jewish butchers,
meat found in the hand of a gentile is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the basis of רבי's reaction in step 3 by tying it to his general ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where the butchers are Jewish, meat found with a gentile is permitted.

steps.title: A second version: the butcher only meant to hurt his rival
steps.stepSummary: Some report רבי's words differently: the fool only meant to upset the other man, so there is no reason to forbid the butcher shops.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רבי said: 'Because of this fool who only meant to hurt his friend, should we forbid all the butcher shops?!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another version of what רבי said. Here the butcher's claim is seen as a spiteful remark, not a real act of selling טְרֵפָה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, the butcher did act improperly, and רבי still does not forbid the meat. In this version, the butcher only said it to cause his rival pain, so his claim is not taken seriously at all. Both versions reach the same result: the butcher shops stay permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: To cause him pain or distress

steps.whatToRemember: Both versions agree on the הלכה: one butcher's story does not forbid the meat in the butcher shops. They differ only on whether the butcher really sold טְרֵפָה or just said it to hurt his rival.

phrases.english: There are those who say: Rabbi said:
Because of this fool
who intended to cause distress to his fellow,
should we forbid all the butcher shops?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different version of רבי's reaction in step 3, reading the butcher's claim as spite rather than fact.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The butcher's claim is treated as a spiteful remark, so the butcher shops stay permitted.

steps.title: Inference from the second version: otherwise the meat would be forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads the second version of רבי's words closely. It infers that if the butcher had not just been trying to upset the other man, the meat would be forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: The reason רבי permitted the meat is that the butcher only meant to upset his friend. So if that were not the case, the meat would be forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is drawing an inference from the second version of רבי's words in step 5. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the second version, רבי gives a specific reason: the fool only wanted to upset the other man. If that reason is needed, then without it the meat would be forbidden. That sounds stricter than רבי's general rule from step 4.

keyTerms.meaning: To cause him distress, to upset him
But if it were not so (an inference from the opposite case)

phrases.english: The reason is that he intended
to upset his fellow;
but if it were not so, it would be forbidden.
phrases.notes: "It" means the meat in the gentile butcher shops.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws an inference from the second version of רבי's words
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without the butcher's intent to upset his friend, the meat would be forbidden.

steps.title: But רבי permits meat found with a gentile
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the inference with a ברייתא. In it, רבי says that where the shops and butchers are Jewish, meat found with a gentile is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned that רבי says: where the butcher shops and butchers are Jewish, meat found in a gentile's hand is permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the inference from step 6. It quotes רבי's own general rule, which permits meat found with a gentile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבי permits meat found with a gentile in a Jewish town, why would he need the special reason that the butcher was only trying to upset his friend? The general rule alone should be enough to permit it.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught: רבי says:
Where the butcher shops and butchers are Jewish,
meat found in a gentile's hand is permitted!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the inference of step 6
steps.kashyaTarget: The inference that without the intent to upset, the meat would be forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי's general rule already permits meat found with a gentile, so no special reason should be needed.

steps.title: Here a forbidden sale was already known
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this case is different. Here it was already known that forbidden meat had been sold to the gentile.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different here, because forbidden meat has already been shown to be present.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It explains why this case needs a special reason even though רבי's general rule is lenient.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי's general rule covers ordinary cases, where we have no reason to suspect anything. In the butcher story, the butcher's own claim puts a forbidden sale to a gentile on record. Because of that, we would worry it happened more than once, unless we say the butcher was just talking to upset his friend.

keyTerms.meaning: Something forbidden has been established, shown to be present

steps.whatToRemember: רבי's leniency for meat found with a gentile applies in ordinary cases. Once forbidden meat is known to be in the picture, we need an extra reason to permit.

phrases.english: It is different here,
since the forbidden thing has been established.
phrases.notes: He means the butcher's claim put a forbidden sale on record, so the general rule alone isn't enough.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי's general rule should permit the meat with no extra reason.
steps.terutzMaskana: Here forbidden meat is known to have been sold, so a special reason is needed.

steps.title: Meat that was out of sight is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that once meat has been out of sight, it is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: Meat that has been hidden from the eye is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new, related topic. It brings רב's rule that meat left out of sight becomes forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since we are talking about meat whose status is unclear, the גמרא brings a general rule. According to רב, once meat has gone unwatched, we can no longer be sure it is the same kosher meat.

keyTerms.meaning: Hidden from the eye, left out of sight and unwatched

steps.whyThisMatters: רב's rule is the basis of the halachic concern about meat left unwatched. The rest of this section tests it against other sources.

phrases.english: רב said: Meat,
once it has been hidden from the eye, is forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב: בָּשָׂר, כֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּתְעַלֵּם מִן הָעַיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a related topic about meat with an unclear status
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Meat that was out of sight is forbidden.

steps.title: Challenge from רבי's rule about meat found with a gentile
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב from רבי's ruling that meat found with a gentile is permitted in a Jewish town.
steps.simpleTranslation: They objected: רבי says, where the butcher shops and butchers are Jewish, meat found in a gentile's hand is permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's rule. It uses the same ברייתא of רבי quoted earlier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Meat in a gentile's hand was surely out of a Jew's sight for a while. Yet רבי permits it. That seems to go against רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Meat found in a gentile's possession

phrases.english: They objected: רבי says:
Where the butcher shops and butchers are Jewish,
meat found in a gentile's hand is permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's rule from step 9
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that meat out of sight is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Meat in a gentile's hand was unwatched by Jews, yet רבי permits it.

steps.title: Meat found with a gentile is different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that meat found in a gentile's hand is a different case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Meat found in a gentile's hand is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב. It says רבי's case is not the kind of case רב was talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב is talking about meat that was left alone and lost from sight - once unwatched, we suspect it was swapped. Meat in a gentile's hand is different because it is בחזקת המשתמר, presumed to have been guarded: the gentile did not slaughter it, and Jewish butchers would not sell him a טרפה to resell here. The case רב forbids is בשר המונח, meat left lying around, which ravens may have swapped. So the only question is where the gentile got it, and in a Jewish town it surely came from Jewish butchers.

phrases.english: Found in a gentile's hand is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי permits meat that was out of sight, which goes against רב.
steps.terutzMaskana: Meat in a gentile's hand was not left unwatched, so רב's rule does not apply.

steps.title: Challenge from the nine kosher stores and one non-kosher store
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that meat found lying around in a town with nine kosher stores and one נְבֵלָה store follows the majority and is permitted. This seems to go against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come hear: There are nine stores selling kosher slaughtered meat and one selling נבלה meat. If a person bought from one of them and doesn't know which, the doubt is forbidden. But with meat that was found, follow the majority.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second challenge to רב. It uses a ברייתא that permits found meat by following the majority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Found meat was obviously out of sight. Still, the ברייתא says to follow the majority of stores, which are kosher, and permit it. That seems to contradict רב, who forbids any meat that was out of sight.

keyTerms.meaning: Meat of a properly slaughtered animal
Meat of an animal that died without proper שחיטה
When in doubt, it is forbidden

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two cases in this ברייתא. Meat bought from an unknown store is forbidden, but meat found lying around follows the majority. The challenge to רב comes only from the second case, the found meat.

phrases.english: Come and hear: Nine stores,
all of them selling meat of slaughtered animals,
and one selling meat of נבלה,
and he bought from one of them
and does not know which of them he bought from:
his doubt is forbidden,
but with found meat, follow the majority.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to רב
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that meat out of sight is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Found meat was out of sight, yet the ברייתא permits it by following the majority.

steps.title: Here too the meat was found with a gentile
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא's "found" meat means meat found in a gentile's hand.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it is talking about meat found in a gentile's hand.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב again, using the same answer as before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא reads "found" in the ברייתא as meat found with a gentile, not meat lying unwatched. So the meat was never really "hidden from the eye," and רב's rule is not affected.

phrases.english: Here too, it is talking about meat found in a gentile's hand.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12 the same way as step 11
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא permits meat found lying unwatched.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא means meat found in a gentile's hand, which was not unwatched.

steps.title: Challenge from raw and cooked meat found in a city
steps.stepSummary: A משנה rules that raw meat found in a city follows the majority of butchers, and cooked meat follows the majority of meat eaters. This seems to permit found meat, against רב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come hear: If one found meat in it, if it is raw, follow the majority of butchers. If it is cooked, follow the majority of meat eaters.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a third challenge to רב. Step 15 shows the earlier answer won't work here, and step 16 gives a new answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This משנה talks about meat simply found in the city, not in a gentile's hand. It still lets us follow the majority, which can permit the meat. This is harder to explain away than the earlier sources.

keyTerms.meaning: The majority of people who eat meat

phrases.english: Come and hear: If one found meat in it,
phrases.notes: "In it" means a city where both Jews and gentiles live, as the משנה describes before this line.

phrases.english: (if raw) follow the majority of butchers,
phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the words in round brackets.

phrases.english: and if it is cooked,
follow the majority of meat eaters.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third challenge to רב
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that meat out of sight is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה follows the majority for meat found in the city, so found meat can be permitted even though it was out of sight.

steps.title: Why not just look who is holding the cooked meat?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא blocks the earlier answer 'found in a gentile's hand'. If someone is holding the meat, we can simply see whether he is a גוי or a Jew, so there is no reason to follow the majority of meat eaters.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say that here too the משנה means the meat was found in a gentile's hand, then why does it say that cooked meat follows the majority of meat eaters? Let us simply look and see whether a גוי or a Jew is holding it!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tests whether the earlier answer ('found in a gentile's hand') can save רב from the משנה in step 14. It shows that this answer does not work here.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 13 the גמרא explained 'found' as 'found in a gentile's hand'. That cannot fit this משנה, because if a person is holding the meat we would just check who he is. We would not need to count the majority of meat eaters in the city.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say; introduces a possible answer that the גמרא is about to reject
The majority of people who eat meat in the town

phrases.english: And if you would say: here too
it is a case where it was found in a gentile's hand,

phrases.aramaic: מְבוּשָּׁל הַלֵּךְ אַחַר רוֹב אוֹכְלֵי בָשָׂר?
phrases.english: then why does it say: cooked meat, follow the majority of meat eaters?
Let us just see: if a gentile is holding it,
or if a Jew is holding it!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: הָכָא נָמֵי בְּנִמְצָא בְּיַד גּוֹי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Strengthens the challenge of step 14 by ruling out the defense that worked in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: Applying the answer 'found in a gentile's hand' to the משנה of raw and cooked meat
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If someone is holding the meat, we can identify him directly, so a rule about following the majority would be pointless.

steps.title: Someone watched the meat the whole time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is about someone who stood and watched the meat from the moment it fell. It never went out of sight, but he does not know who dropped it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here, what case are we dealing with? A case where someone stood and watched it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new way to read the משנה so it no longer conflicts with רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The meat never went out of sight, so רב's worry about meat that was hidden from view does not apply. The watcher only does not know whether a Jew or a גוי dropped it, so we follow the majority of the town.

keyTerms.meaning: Here, what case are we dealing with? Used to narrow a source to a specific situation
Where someone is standing and watching it

phrases.english: Here, what are we dealing with?
A case where someone is standing and watching it.
phrases.notes: He watched the meat after it fell, but did not see who dropped it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of steps 14–15 with a different case definition.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to permit meat that had gone out of sight, which goes against רב.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה speaks of meat that was watched the whole time, so רב's rule is not involved.

steps.title: Challenge from meat found outside ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: A משנה rules that whole limbs found in the outlying areas are נבלה, but small pieces are permitted. The 'someone was watching' answer cannot work here, because then why would the limbs be called נבלה?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: meat found in the outlying areas: whole limbs are נבלות, but pieces are permitted. And if you would say that here too someone stood and watched it, then why are the limbs considered נבלות?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new source that seems to permit meat that went out of sight, which goes against רב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The pieces are permitted even though they lay unwatched, and that contradicts רב. The answer from step 16 cannot help. If someone had watched the meat, there would be no reason to call the whole limbs נבלה, so the משנה must be about meat that was not watched.

keyTerms.meaning: Carcasses of animals that were not slaughtered properly

steps.confusionAlert: The question 'why are limbs נבלה?' is not a question about limbs themselves. It proves that nobody was watching, so the permission for the pieces really does go against רב.

phrases.english: Come and hear: if meat was found in the outlying areas,
phrases.notes: This משנה is in שקלים. It means any place outside ירושלים.

phrases.english: whole limbs are carcasses,
pieces are permitted.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי תֵּימָא: הָכָא נָמֵי בְּעוֹמֵד וְרוֹאֵהוּ,
phrases.english: And if you would say: here too it is where someone stood and watched it,
then why are the limbs carcasses?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new challenge to רב, built so that the step 16 answer cannot be used.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that meat which went out of sight is forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Unwatched pieces are permitted, and the 'watching' explanation cannot apply because then the limbs would not be called נבלה.

steps.title: רב reads 'permitted' as not נבלה, not as allowed to eat
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that this משנה is only a problem for רב, and רב already explained it: the pieces are 'permitted' only in that they are not treated as נבלה. לוי holds they may even be eaten.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this a difficulty for anyone but רב? But it was already said about this משנה: רב said they are permitted as far as נבלה goes, and לוי said they are permitted to eat.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that רב himself read this משנה in a way that fits his rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, 'permitted' only means the pieces do not have the status of נבלה. They do not make a person impure, and eating them does not bring lashes. They still may not be eaten, because they went out of sight. לוי disagrees and allows eating them, so the משנה is no proof against רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Is there a problem only according to...? Used to say a source was already explained by that very opinion
Free from the status of נבלה, but not necessarily allowed to eat

steps.whatToRemember: There are two levels of 'permitted': free from נבלה status (רב), or fully allowed to eat (לוי).

phrases.english: Is this a difficulty for anyone other than רב?
phrases.notes: Literally, 'Is the reason anything but for רב?' The question only works against רב, and רב already dealt with it.

phrases.english: But it was already stated about it:
רב said: they are permitted as far as being a carcass goes,
phrases.notes: He means the pieces do not count as נבלה, but they still may not be eaten.

phrases.english: and לוי said: they are permitted to be eaten.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17 by citing רב's own reading of that משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting a word in the source ('permitted')
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Permitted' means the pieces may be eaten, which goes against רב.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רב, 'permitted' means only free from נבלה status. Eating is still forbidden.

steps.title: רב's rule was learned by inference
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רב never stated outright that meat which went out of sight is forbidden. His rule was inferred from something else.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this ruling of רב was not stated explicitly. Rather, it was stated by inference.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds background about the source of רב's rule and sets up the story that will show how it was inferred.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the discussion treated רב's rule as an explicit statement. Now we learn it was only deduced from an incident involving him, which prepares the ground for the story about רב at the river.

keyTerms.meaning: By inference, deduced from something else
Meat that went out of sight; the subject of רב's rule

steps.whyThisMatters: A rule that comes from inference can later be questioned by asking whether the inference was correct.

phrases.english: And this ruling of רב,
phrases.notes: This is his rule that meat which went out of sight is forbidden.

phrases.english: was not stated explicitly,
rather, it was stated by inference.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא דְּרַב, לָאו בְּפֵירוּשׁ אִתְּמַר, אֶלָּא מִכְּלָלָא אִתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from defending רב's rule to explaining where the rule comes from.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב's rule about meat that went out of sight was deduced, not said outright.

steps.title: The story begins: רב at the river ford
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins the story from which רב's rule was inferred. רב was sitting at the ford of a river and saw a certain man doing something.
steps.simpleTranslation: For רב was sitting at the ford of the אישתטיא river, and he saw a certain man who was...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts telling the story behind the inference. The sentence continues in the next part of the daf.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This story is the evidence for רב's rule. What רב saw and how he reacted will show why people concluded that he forbids meat that went out of sight.

phrases.english: For רב was sitting
at the ford of the Ishtatya river,
he saw a certain man
who was...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the story that step 19 promised as the source of רב's rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The story of רב at the river is the source of the inference about his rule.
